processing: A factory blend of sun-dried maocha from several grades, steamed and pressed into cakes, with younger, more tippy material than the 7542 recipe.
harvest_season: A blended recipe, so no single picking defines it; each batch is identified by year and batch number.
appearance_dry: A cake with fine pale buds scattered evenly across the surface among dark green leaf.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow when young, deepening to amber and then red-brown with age.
appearance_wet: Mostly small, tender leaf and buds, finer than in 7542.
taste_profile: Finer and more tender than 7542, with a thick broth and a sweet aftertaste; young batches keep the usual sheng bitterness.

brewing.notes: Bud-rich blends extract fast, so keep early steeps very short on young cakes.

vintage_note: Sold by year and batch number, and collectors treat them as different teas. Recent batches are bought young to drink or store, while older cakes trade on age and storage, with 1980s thick-paper wrapped examples reaching auction houses. Forgeries of old factory cakes are a concern, so provenance matters more than the printed year.
description:
7532 is one of the classic recipe numbers of the Menghai Tea Factory, whose modern brand is Dayi. It is the more tender sibling of 7542: a blend built around younger leaf and more buds, aiming for finesse rather than force.

Like all recipe cakes, it is a matter of blending. The factory combines grades of maocha, then steams and presses them. By the usual reading of the code, 75 points to the year the recipe began, 3 to the average leaf grade and 2 to the factory, Menghai.

Expect a thick, smooth broth with a good sweet return, and bitterness that is present but less insistent than in 7542. Being bud-heavy, it extracts quickly, so short steeps are the main thing to get right.

Collectors call the cake Xueyin, or Snow Seal, a name said to have been coined by a collector for the pale buds scattered over its face. Always buy by year and batch: the number on the wrapper is a recipe, and the leaf inside has changed over the decades.
history:
Menghai Tea Factory traces itself to the Fohai experimental tea factory set up at the end of the 1930s. The recipe code suggests a 1975 start, though that reading rests on trade convention and no factory record of the first batch has been traced.

The 1980s thick-paper cakes are the best-known early examples. One auction description says they used mainly young grade-three leaf, with buds that were scarce and costly, keeping output small.
